slides.title: Exploitation of Approximation and Sparsity for LoRA Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices
paragraphs: Good afternoon, everyone.
I'm Sheng-Fang Hsu from National Central University.
Today I will present our work, "Exploitation of Approximation and Sparsity for LoRA Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices." This is joint work with Li-Peng Wu and Professor Pei-Yun Tsai.

slides.title: Contents
paragraphs: Here is the outline.
After the introduction and motivation, I will introduce three main techniques: the sparsity-inducing SiLU, the coarse-grained sparse update, and the DFP12 format.
After that, I'll briefly cover how we handle the cross-entropy loss, and finally, I will show the experimental results.

slides.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Let me begin with the background.
Our baseline is QA-LoRA.
The pretrained weights are stored as integers with group-wise quantization, and only the two low-rank adapters, W-A and W-B, are trained in floating point.
The input is summed within each group of size G, so the adapter is very small.
After fine-tuning, the adapter can be merged into the zero point, so inference stays fully in integer.
In this work, we use rank sixteen and group size thirty-two.

slides.title: Motivation
paragraphs: Fine-tuning on edge devices faces three main challenges.
The first is memory: backpropagation must store activations and gradients, which puts pressure on both memory size and bandwidth.
The second is nonlinearity: functions like SiLU and the exponential need dedicated hardware.
And the third is compute: matrix multiplications take most of the MAC operations.
So our goal is to build one framework that addresses all three challenges together.

slides.title: SI-SiLU Approximation (1/2)
paragraphs: Let me start with our most important technique, the sparsity-inducing SiLU, or SI-SiLU.
It is a piecewise-linear approximation with no multipliers, and it has three paths.
When the input is below minus zero point five, the output is simply zero.
When the input is above zero point five, the output is the input itself.
In between, we use eight segments stored in a small look-up table.
To choose the path, the range classifier only needs to check the sign bit and the exponent bits.
Inside the table, each slope is a sum of two powers of two, so multiplying by a slope becomes shift-and-add.
This also lowers the cost of gradient propagation.
Moreover, since each segment is linear, its derivative is just its slope.
As a result, the activation and its derivative can share the same look-up table.

slides.title: SI-SiLU Approximation (2/3)
paragraphs: Next, this figure shows where the sparsity is induced.
The red line is our approximated SiLU, and the orange line is its derivative.
Below minus zero point five, both the output and the gradient are exactly zero.
By the chain rule, these zeros propagate through backpropagation, so those elements can simply be skipped.
For comparison, ReSiLU2 is shown in green.
Its derivative is non-zero all the way down to minus six point three, so it produces almost no sparsity.
At the same time, our derivative is more accurate, with a mean squared error of zero point four nine percent, versus one point seven percent for ReSiLU2.

slides.title: SI-SiLU Approximation (3/3)
paragraphs: But how much sparsity can we actually get?
To answer this, we analyzed real data layer by layer, and we found that the sparsity depends strongly on depth.
The shallow layers, zero to seven, have only zero point seven two percent, but the deep layers, fifteen to twenty-one, reach twenty-one point eight seven percent on average.
The table then compares our design with previous work.
First, because of the zero region, our design can induce sparsity.
Second, shift-and-add reduces the computation of gradient propagation.
And third, both the SiLU output and its derivative come from the look-up table with simple computation, so no extra memory is needed.

slides.title: Coarse-Grained Sparse Update (1/2)
paragraphs: The second technique is the coarse-grained sparse update.
In LoRA, backpropagation has two parts.
The adapter gradient is only the computation for updating the LoRA weights A and B themselves.
The activation gradient is the gradient with respect to the input.
It becomes the upstream gradient of the previous matrix, so it is the cost of preparing the gradient for the next step back.
This chart shows the cost of each matrix in one decoding layer.
The orange part is the adapter gradient.
It is tiny, because the rank is small.
The blue part is the activation gradient propagation, and it is cumulative: to reach a matrix, the gradient must first pass through every matrix after it, starting from the layer output.
That is why it is almost zero at D, the down projection, but grows to about twenty-four G-MACs at Q and K.
In other words, the propagation clearly dominates the cost.
Therefore, lowering the rank further does not help much.
To make LoRA efficient in hardware, we must reduce propagation.

slides.title: Coarse-Grained Sparse Update (2/2)
paragraphs: So how can we reduce propagation?
There are two ways.
In a matrix-wise sparse update, we skip some matrices, but the gradient must still travel through every layer to reach the lower ones.
In contrast, in a layer-wise update, we freeze the first S layers, so backpropagation simply stops at layer S plus one, and all the cross-layer propagation below it is gone.
Therefore, we adopt the layer-wise update.
In addition, it works well together with SI-SiLU.
As we saw earlier, the shallow layers have little sparsity.
By freezing them, the average induced sparsity of SI-SiLU rises from about eleven percent to fifteen percent for BoolQ and XSum, and to eighteen percent for WinoGrande.

slides.title: DFP12 Format (1/2)
paragraphs: The third technique is the data format underneath everything, DFP12.

In language model fine-tuning, compared with the pre-trained weights and the activations, the gradients are the most sensitive to the data format, because their values change a lot from layer to layer.
As this figure shows, the gradient distribution is not uniform across layers, so it is hard to cover all of them with one fixed dynamic range.
To handle this, DFP12 uses a five-bit exponent and a six-bit mantissa.
More importantly, its exponent bias is dynamic: it is set by the largest exponent in each matrix.
So, unlike the red box, which has a fixed range, the gray window moves with the data and covers almost the whole range.

slides.title: DFP12 Format (2/2)
paragraphs: In the datapath, for faster simulation, we use BF16 as a container, and quantize the result to DFP12 after each operation.
The mantissa uses round-to-nearest.
In this way, our simulation captures the quantization error and still keeps the accumulation error.
For the hardware cost, we synthesized the MAC unit in twenty-eight nanometers.
Compared with BF16, the DFP12 MAC unit saves sixteen point eight percent area and fourteen point eight percent energy per MAC.

slides.title: Task-Adaptive KCE for CE Backward
paragraphs: Finally, the cross-entropy loss.
Every token produces a dense logit gradient.
Top-K selection itself is a standard technique.
What we do is apply it to the cross-entropy backward during fine-tuning, so each token keeps only K-CE values plus the label.
For BoolQ, that is nine out of thirty-two thousand.
The key point is that K-CE must follow the task.
It depends on the number of loss tokens, meaning the tokens that are not masked out and count in the loss.
For example, WinoGrande uses prompt masking, so very few tokens count in the loss, and it needs a larger K-CE.

slides.title: Experimental Setup
paragraphs: Now let's move to the experiments.
We fine-tune TinyLlama one point one B with QA-LoRA, and the weights, activations, and gradients all use the DFP12 format.
As the golden reference, we use PyTorch autograd in BF16.
We evaluate three tasks.
BoolQ is a yes-or-no question answering task, and WinoGrande is a commonsense reasoning task.
Both are evaluated with the standard lm-evaluation-harness.
In addition, to check that our framework also generalizes beyond question answering, we test XSum, which is a text generation task.

slides.title: Simulation Results
paragraphs: This figure shows a cumulative ablation on BoolQ, WinoGrande, and XSum.

From left to right, we add each technique step by step: starting from the BF16 baseline as the golden reference, then the DFP12 format, then the nonlinear approximation, and finally the sparsity strategies.
The lines show accuracy for the first two tasks and ROUGE-L for XSum.
As you can see, they stay stable through the whole process, and the final result is within one percent of the BF16 baseline.
Meanwhile, the bars show the MAC savings, which mainly come from our sparsity strategies.
Among them, the coarse-grained update gives the biggest gain, because it stops gradient propagation early.
Moreover, our framework is not limited to question answering.
On the generative task XSum, ROUGE-L even improves, from twenty-nine point eight four to thirty-one point two eight.

slides.title: Cross-Task Results
paragraphs: Here are the final settings and results for each task.
Across tasks, only two settings change: the freeze depth and K-CE.
We tune them for each task, based on the number of loss tokens and how much the task relies on basic semantic information.
For example, WinoGrande has fewer loss tokens, so we set K-CE to two hundred fifty-six and freeze eleven layers.
This gives the largest saving, fifty-eight point five percent of the MACs.
For BoolQ and XSum, the savings are forty-one point one and thirty-eight point two percent.

slides.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: To conclude, first, SI-SiLU creates sparsity for inputs below minus zero point five without multipliers, and with lower error than ReSiLU2.
Second, the layer-wise coarse-grained update removes propagation in the shallow layers, and it complements SI-SiLU.
Third, DFP12 serves as the data format underneath, saving sixteen point eight percent area and fourteen point eight percent energy.
Overall, with these techniques together, our framework reduces fine-tuning MACs by up to fifty-eight point five percent, with less than one percent degradation.

slides.title: Thank You — Questions?
paragraphs: Thank you for your attention.
I'm happy to take any questions.

qa.note: Q&A 2 分鐘。先說 Thank you for the question，聽不懂就請對方再說一次。

items.q: How did you choose K-CE and the freeze depth S?
items.zh: K-CE 離線看 softmax 前 K 個的累積機率；S 用小批次測任務對淺層語意的敏感度
a: For K-CE, we decide it offline.
We check the cumulative probability of the top-K softmax outputs in the forward pass.
For example, if the top eight cover about ninety percent, we set K-CE to eight.
For S, we run short tests on a small batch, to see how much the task depends on basic semantics in the shallow layers.
A more systematic way to choose S is part of our future work.

items.zh: 換不同模型、不同任務，檢查強健性與泛用性
a: We plan to test other models and more tasks,
to check the robustness and generality of our framework.

items.q: Have you implemented this on hardware? How much real speedup do you get, since the SI-SiLU sparsity is irregular?
items.zh: 除了資料格式，其他硬體還在進行；難在整合微調資料流；稀疏度目前靠分析輸入判別
a: Not yet. Except for the DFP12 MAC unit, the hardware is still in progress.
The main challenge is integrating it into the whole fine-tuning dataflow.
Right now, the SI-SiLU sparsity is detected by checking the inputs.
The hardware for it will be decided after the fine-tuning control flow is finalized.

items.q: Why DFP12 instead of FP8 or MX formats? And what is the overhead of finding the maximum exponent?
items.zh: 兼顧效能並省記憶體與頻寬；試過 FP8 效果不好；找最大指數的成本比矩陣乘法小很多
a: Our goal is to fine-tune with good accuracy, while saving memory and bandwidth.
We did try FP8, but it did not work well in our framework.
Finding the maximum exponent is very cheap compared with the matrix multiplication itself,
so the overhead is acceptable.

items.q: Real SiLU is negative below zero. Does setting it to zero hurt the forward output? Do you use SI-SiLU in the forward pass?
items.zh: 正向用原本的 SiLU、輸出不存；反向時用 SI-SiLU 即時重算輸出和導數，所以只影響反向
a: In the forward pass, we keep the original SiLU, so the forward output is not changed.
We don't store the SiLU output.
In backpropagation, we recompute it on the fly with SI-SiLU,
and the derivative comes from the same look-up table.
So the approximation only affects the backward pass.

items.q: Will these results hold for larger models, like LLaMA 7B?
items.zh: 這是未來想繼續探討的
a: That's a good question.
Larger models like LLaMA 7B are what we want to explore next.

items.q: Memory is your first challenge, but you mainly show MAC savings. How much memory do you save?
items.zh: 記憶體依賴 QA-LoRA，不是我們的成果所以沒分析；凍結 S 層也不用存那些層的激活值
a: For memory, we rely on QA-LoRA.
It's a method we adopt, not our contribution, so we did not analyze the final memory saving.
Also, by freezing the first S layers, we don't need to store their activations for backpropagation.

items.q: How is freezing the first S layers different from only fine-tuning the top layers, or methods like LISA?
items.zh: 差在梯度傳播成本：凍結可以中斷梯度傳播，省大量運算和激活值儲存；又跟 SI-SiLU 互補
a: The key point is the cost of gradient propagation.
By freezing the first S layers, the gradient stops at layer S plus one.
This removes a lot of computation, and the storage of forward activations.
It also works well with SI-SiLU, because the shallow layers have little sparsity.

items.q: What edge device are you targeting? What is the power or memory budget?
items.zh: 未來會在晶片上跑，實際裝置還在研究
a: We plan to run it on a chip in the future,
but we are still studying the actual target device.
